note: Guided lesson scripts. Beats restate what the section already teaches, in a register that reads aloud. Code is verbatim from textbook.json. Every question is answerable from the beats above it and carries a concept for drilling.

beats.say: Welcome. By the end of this lesson you will have written a program and watched it answer you back. If you have never written code before, you are in exactly the right place.
Start with what a script actually is. A script is a list of instructions that you write and the computer follows, one at a time, from the top of the file to the bottom.
That is genuinely all it is. There is no hidden machinery underneath, and you do not need to understand how a computer works to start telling one what to do.

Luau is the language Roblox uses for those instructions. When you write Luau, you are writing the rules of your game: what happens when a player touches something, what a button does, how a score goes up.
The first instruction you will meet is print. You hand it something, and it shows that something to you.
That sounds small. It is the single most useful thing you can do while learning, because it is how you get the computer to tell you what it is thinking.
Here is your first program. Two lines, two ideas.
beats.code:
local message = "LuauX online"
print(message)

beats.say: The first line takes the text LuauX online and gives it a name: message. The text is now stored somewhere, under a label you chose.
The second line hands that name to print. Print looks up what message holds and shows it to you.
Notice that the second line never mentions the text itself. It only mentions the name. That separation is the whole point: change the value in one place and everything that uses the name follows.
Now the experiment. Run it once unchanged and read the output. Then change only the words between the quotation marks and run it again.
Say out loud what changed and what stayed the same. The instructions did not change. The text you handed to them did.
One thing worth saying before you start. The Practice runner in this app is a sandbox. Nothing you type there can break your computer, your Roblox account, or a real game.
You cannot get it wrong in a way that matters. Type things, run them, see what happens, and break it on purpose if you like. That is how this is meant to be used.

questions.ask: In what order does Luau follow the instructions in a script?
options: Top to bottom, one at a time
questions.explain: Luau runs each instruction in order, finishing one before starting the next.

questions.ask: What does print do?
options: Sends the text to a printer
Shows a value so you can see it
Saves the value to a file
questions.explain: print makes an otherwise invisible value visible. In Roblox Studio it writes to the Output window.

questions.ask: What does this program show?
questions.explain: The name greeting holds the text Hello, and print shows what is in it.

questions.ask: You are worried about typing something wrong in Practice. What can happen?
options: It could break your Roblox account
Nothing. It is a sandbox, so experiment freely
questions.explain: The runner is isolated. Getting it wrong is how you learn, and it costs nothing.

questions.ask: Fill in the missing word: print makes an otherwise invisible value ___.
questions.explain: print is for making an invisible value visible. In Roblox Studio it writes to the Output window.

questions.ask: Put these events in the order Luau follows them.
options: Luau runs the local instruction and gives the text the name greeting.
The value Hello becomes visible in the output.
questions.explain: Luau follows instructions from top to bottom. The name exists before print uses it, and print then makes its value visible.

beats.say: The goal here is narrow and worth having: look at a line of Luau and confidently say which part is a name you invented, which part is plain text, and which part is punctuation doing a job.
When you look at a line of code it can feel like one solid blob of symbols. It is not. Every line is made of a few kinds of piece, and once you can tell them apart, code stops looking like noise.
Three kinds are worth knowing right now.
Names are labels you invent, like playerName. They point at a value or a function so you can refer to it later.
Text values sit inside quotation marks, like the word Ari in quotes. The quotation marks are a fence: everything inside is taken literally, exactly as written.
Punctuation, such as brackets and the two dots that join text together, groups things and says how they relate.
Here is all three in two lines.
beats.code:
local playerName = "Ari"
print("Welcome, " .. playerName)

beats.say: On the first line, playerName is a name you invented. The word in quotation marks is a text value. Everything else is punctuation doing its job.
On the second line there are two pieces of text either side of the two dots. The two dots join them into one longer piece of text, which is then handed to print.
Notice that the text in quotes includes a trailing space after the comma. That space is inside the fence, so it is taken literally, which is what keeps the two words apart in the output.
Here is the practical payoff. When something goes wrong in a first script, it is almost never anything deep.
It is a misspelled name, a missing quotation mark, or an unclosed bracket. You do not need to know how the language is built internally to find those. You just need to tell the pieces apart.

questions.ask: What tells Luau that something is text rather than a name?
options: It is longer than one word
questions.explain: Quotation marks are the fence. Inside them, everything is taken literally.

questions.ask: You created a name called playerName, then wrote PlayerName. What happens?
questions.explain: Names are case sensitive. PlayerName and playerName are two different names.

questions.ask: This reports that a name cannot be found. Which line is wrong?
options: Line 2, PlayerName does not match playerName
questions.explain: Line 1 created playerName. Line 2 asks for PlayerName, which was never created.

questions.ask: What does this show?
questions.explain: The two dots join the greeting and the name into one piece of text.

questions.ask: Your script fails. What is the most useful next step?
options: Change several things and run it once
Change one thing, run it, then repeat
Start the file again from scratch
Read the whole language grammar first
questions.explain: Changing one thing at a time is how you learn which change mattered. It is how professionals debug, not a beginner crutch.

beats.say: Almost every game needs to remember things: how many coins a player has, whether a door is open, what round it is.
In code you remember something by giving it a name and putting a value in it. That pairing is called a variable.
The word local in front of the name is not decoration. It decides where that name exists.
A name created with local lives inside the block it was declared in, and nowhere else. A block is any chunk between a keyword and its matching end, such as the body of an if.
That sounds like a restriction, and it is, deliberately.
Keeping names contained means you can look at a piece of code and see everything it depends on without hunting through the rest of the file.

It also stops two unrelated parts of a game accidentally writing to the same value and corrupting each other. Both problems get genuinely painful in a real game, so the habit is worth building now while everything is small.
Here is a value being stored and then changed.
beats.code:
local coins = 25
local pickupAmount = 5

coins += pickupAmount
print("Coins: " .. coins)

beats.say: The first two lines each give a name to a number. The third line adds one to the other and stores the result back into coins.
Read that third line as: take what coins already holds, add pickupAmount to it, and put the answer back under the same name.
Now the boundary. Watch what happens to a name declared inside a block once the block ends.
beats.code:
if true then
    local bonus = 10
    print(bonus)
end

print(bonus)

beats.say: The first print works, because it sits inside the same block where bonus was declared. The second one is outside that block, and the name does not exist there.
That is not a bug in the language. It is the containment doing exactly what it was asked to do.

questions.ask: What does local decide about a name?
options: Where in the code it exists
What type of value it holds
questions.explain: local confines the name to the block it was declared in.

questions.ask: The second print fails. Why?
questions.code:
if true then
    local bonus = 10
    print(bonus)
end

print(bonus)
options: bonus was never given a value
bonus only exists inside the if block
The if block is missing an end
questions.explain: bonus lives between then and end. After end, that name is gone.

questions.ask: What does this show?
questions.explain: Plus equals takes what is already in coins and adds to it.

questions.ask: Code after an if block needs a value that the block calculates. What should you do?
options: Declare the name before the block, assign inside it
Declare it inside the block with local
Use print to carry the value out
questions.explain: Decide where the value needs to be visible, and declare it there.

beats.say: The aim here is to write an arithmetic expression that produces the number you actually intended, and to use brackets to say so out loud.
When one line contains several operations, Luau does not simply work left to right. It follows a fixed order, the same one you were taught in school.
Multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction. So two plus three times four is fourteen, not twenty.
The multiplication goes first regardless of where it sits in the line. Its position does not buy it priority; its kind does.
Brackets override that order. Anything inside brackets is worked out first, so two plus three, in brackets, times four is twenty.
This matters more than it sounds. Reward formulas, damage calculations and prices are exactly the kind of thing where a quietly wrong number is hard to notice and annoying to track down later.
Here is a reward being calculated with the order made explicit.
beats.code:
local baseReward = 20
local multiplier = 2
local bonus = 5
local reward = (baseReward * multiplier) + bonus
print("Reward: " .. reward)

beats.say: The brackets around the multiplication are not strictly needed here, because multiplication would have gone first anyway.
They are there because they state the intent. A reader does not have to remember the rule to know what you meant.
So a practical habit: when a calculation has more than two parts, add the brackets even when the default order already does what you want.
You are writing for the person who reads this in a month, and that person is usually you.

questions.ask: What is the value of this expression?
questions.explain: Multiplication happens before addition, so it is 2 plus 12.

questions.ask: And this one?
questions.explain: The brackets force the addition first, then multiply by four.

questions.ask: Why does adding the text twenty to the number five fail?
options: Text and numbers are different kinds of value
questions.explain: Quotation marks make it text. Adding text to a number is not meaningful, so Luau stops.

questions.ask: Your formula has four parts and the default order already gives the right answer. Should you add brackets?
options: Yes, they state the intent for the next reader
Only if the answer is wrong
questions.explain: Brackets cost nothing and remove a whole category of quiet mistakes.

beats.say: Alongside numbers and text there is a third kind of value, and it has only two possibilities: true and false.
It is called a boolean, and it is what every decision in your game ultimately comes down to. Is the door powered? Does the player have the key? Is the round over?
Two words let you combine them.
The word and is true only when both sides are true. Both conditions must hold.
The word or is true when at least one side is true.
Here is a door that needs both a key and power. Two conditions, one decision.
beats.code:
local hasKey = false
local isDoorPowered = true
local canOpen = hasKey and isDoorPowered

if canOpen then
    print("Door opened")
else
    print("Find the key first")
end

beats.say: Look at the third line. The combined condition is given a name: canOpen. That name is the part worth copying.
Naming the combination pays off immediately. A name like canOpen tells the next reader what the condition means.
Repeating the raw condition in three places instead tells them nothing, and means fixing the rule later requires finding all three.
In this run hasKey is false, so the and is false whatever the power is, and the door stays shut. Change hasKey to true and the same code takes the other branch.

questions.ask: hasKey is false and isDoorPowered is true. What is hasKey and isDoorPowered?
questions.explain: and needs both sides to be true. One false makes the whole thing false.

questions.ask: Same values, but now hasKey or isDoorPowered. What is the result?
questions.explain: or needs only one side to be true, and isDoorPowered is true.

questions.ask: Why store a combined condition in a name like canOpen?
options: It says what the condition means, and the rule lives in one place
questions.explain: The name carries the meaning, and changing the rule later means changing one line, not three.

questions.ask: When does the compact and-or pattern for choosing a value go wrong?
options: When the middle value is false
When it is inside a function
questions.explain: A false middle value hands control to the or branch, so the result is always the second value.

beats.say: Up to now every script has run straight through, top to bottom. Real games need to react differently to different situations, and that means branching.
There are two shapes for making a choice, and they look similar enough to be worth separating carefully.
The familiar shape is the if statement: when the condition holds, run this block of instructions, otherwise run that one.
Use it when the two paths do different things.
Luau also has an if, then, else expression. That is a different tool. Instead of running a block, it produces a single value that you can store in a name.
Use it when both paths produce a value and the only question is which one.
Here both shapes appear together, doing related work, so you can compare them directly.
beats.code:
local health = 40

local status = if health <= 0 then "Respawning" else "Active"

if health <= 0 then
    print("Disable player input")
else
    print("Keep playing")
end

print("Status: " .. status)

beats.say: The middle line produces a value. It picks one of two pieces of text and stores the winner under the name status. Nothing is done, something is chosen.
The block below it acts. Each branch runs a different instruction. Nothing is stored, something happens.
That is the distinction, and it is worth getting right early: statements act, expressions produce.
Choosing the shape that matches your intent is most of what makes branching code readable.

questions.ask: You want to choose between two values and store the result. Which fits?
questions.explain: The expression produces a value, so it can sit on the right of an assignment.

questions.ask: This reports a missing end. Why?
questions.code:
if health <= 0 then
    print("Respawning")
else if health < 20 then
    print("Low health")
end
options: else if as two words starts a new if that needs its own end
print cannot be used inside if
questions.explain: Two words nests a fresh if statement. The single word elseif continues the chain and needs no extra end.

questions.ask: What is the difference between a statement and an expression here?
options: Statements act, expressions produce a value
questions.explain: An if statement runs a block. An if then else expression evaluates to one of two values.

questions.ask: health is 10. What does this show?
questions.code:
local health = 10
if health <= 0 then
    print("Down")
elseif health < 20 then
    print("Low")
else
    print("Fine")
end
questions.explain: The first condition is false, the second is true, so exactly one branch runs.

beats.say: If you need to spawn three rewards, you could write the same instruction three times. If you need three hundred, you cannot.
A loop lets you write the instruction once and say how many times to run it.
A numeric for loop counts. You give it a starting number and an ending number, and it runs the block once for each value.
The current number is available inside the block, under a name you choose.
Here is the simplest useful thing a loop can do.
beats.code:
for rewardNumber = 1, 3 do
    print("Spawn reward #" .. rewardNumber)
end

beats.say: One instruction is written. Three lines come out, and they differ only in the number, because rewardNumber holds a different value on each pass.
A while loop is the other shape. It keeps going as long as its condition stays true.
That makes it more flexible and more dangerous, because something inside the loop has to eventually make that condition false.
If nothing does, the loop never ends. A loop that never finishes is a bug, not a mystery.
So the rule of thumb: reach for for when you know how many times. Reach for while when you are waiting for a situation to change.

questions.ask: You need to do something exactly ten times. Which loop fits best?
questions.explain: for manages its own counter, so it cannot run away from you.

questions.ask: This loop never finishes. What is missing?
questions.code:
local count = 0
while count < 3 do
    print(count)
end
options: A line inside that changes count
questions.explain: The condition checks count, but nothing inside the loop ever changes it.

questions.ask: How many lines does this print?
questions.explain: It runs once for each value from 1 to 4.

questions.ask: You have just written a while loop. What should you check immediately?
options: Which line inside will make the condition false
That the condition uses a number
That it is inside a function
questions.explain: If you cannot point at the line that ends the loop, it will not end.

beats.say: So far each name has held a single value. A table lets one name hold many.
That is how you represent the kinds of collections games are full of: the pickups in a level, the players in a round, the items in an inventory.
A list is written with curly brackets and commas. Three pieces of text in curly brackets is a list of three items.
Each one sits at a numbered position, and the numbering starts at one.
To visit every item you use a for, in loop. On each pass it hands you two things: the position, and the value at that position.
You choose the names for both. That is why the code below says index and pickup rather than anything the language imposed on you.
beats.code:
local pickups = {"Coin", "Gem", "Key"}

for index, pickup in pickups do
    print(index .. ": " .. pickup)
end

beats.say: Run it and match each output line back to an item in the list. The first pass has index one and pickup Coin, and so on down the list.
Then add a fourth item to the list and run it again. You do not touch the loop. The loop already says every item, however many that turns out to be.
That is the payoff of a loop over a list: the code stops depending on how much data there is.

questions.ask: In a Luau list, what position does the first item sit at?
questions.explain: The array convention counts up from 1, not 0.

questions.ask: What two things does a for in loop over a list hand you on each pass?
questions.explain: You choose the names for both, which is why they can be called index and pickup.

questions.ask: You add a fourth item to the list. What has to change in the loop?
questions.explain: The loop asks the table how far it goes, so the code stops depending on the count.

questions.ask: What does the first line of output look like?
questions.code:
local items = {"Coin", "Gem"}

for index, item in items do
    print(index .. ": " .. item)
end
questions.explain: The first pass gives position 1 and the value Coin, joined by the two dots.

beats.say: A list is the right shape when order matters and position is meaningful. A lot of game data is not like that.
Settings, player stats and configuration are collections where each value has a name, not a position. Nobody wants to remember that the volume is item number two.
A table can do this too. Instead of listing values, you write name equals value pairs.
Now you fetch the volume by asking for volume, which is both harder to get wrong and much easier to read six months later.
Here are three settings of three different kinds: a true-or-false, a number, and some text.
beats.code:
local settings = {music = true, volume = 0.7, difficulty = "normal"}

for key, value in settings do
    print(key .. ": " .. tostring(value))
end

beats.say: The same for, in loop walks these as well. What changes is what it hands you: instead of a position and a value, you get the key and the value.
One warning that matters. Unlike a list, these have no guaranteed order.
Do not rely on them coming back in the order you wrote them. If your code needs a particular order, a table with names is the wrong shape for it.
You can also reach a single setting directly by name, without looping at all.
beats.code: print("Volume: " .. settings.volume)

beats.say: Looping is for when you want all of them. Naming one is for when you want that one. Both read clearly, which is the entire reason to store settings this way.

questions.ask: You are storing a player's coins, level and title. Which shape fits?
questions.explain: Names carry the meaning. A position would force every reader to remember an unwritten convention.

questions.ask: You loop over a table with named keys. What can you rely on about the order?
options: It matches the order you wrote them
Nothing, the order is not guaranteed
questions.explain: Keyed entries have no inherent order. If order matters, you wanted a list.

questions.ask: Why is tostring needed when joining a number onto text?
options: To convert it into text so it can be joined
questions.explain: Joining works on text. tostring converts other kinds of value into text first.

questions.ask: You need one specific setting and you know its name. What is the better approach?
options: Loop over everything and stop when you find it
Fetch it directly with a dot and the key
Convert the table to a list first
questions.explain: Loop to visit everything, reach for the key when you want one thing.

beats.say: So far your scripts have run one instruction after another, top to bottom.
A function lets you take a chunk of that work, give it a name, and run it whenever you want, as many times as you want.
Two words do the heavy lifting. Parameters are what the function takes in. Return values are what it hands back.
A vending machine is a fair picture of it. You put something in, something specific comes out, and you do not need to know what happens inside to use it.
Here is the coin counter from Section 2, with the logic given a name.
beats.code:
local function awardCoins(currentCoins: number, pickupAmount: number): number
    return currentCoins + pickupAmount
end

local coins = 25
coins = awardCoins(coins, 5)
print("Coins: " .. coins)

beats.say: Read the first line as the contract. It takes two numbers in, and the number after the closing bracket says it hands a number back.
The body does one thing: it works out the new total and returns it. It does not touch coins. It does not know coins exists.
The important line is the one that calls it. The result is handed back and stored, which is why coins ends up holding the new value.
Now the habit worth building from your very first function. When a function needs to change something, prefer handing back the new value over quietly reaching out and modifying something far away.
Watch what happens when the result is thrown away.
beats.code:
local coins = 25
awardCoins(coins, 5)
print(coins)

beats.say: The function ran. It worked out the right answer. Nobody caught it, so coins is unchanged and the output is the old number.
A function that takes inputs and returns a result can be tested on its own, reused somewhere else, and later moved into a ModuleScript without dragging hidden dependencies along.

questions.ask: What are parameters and return values?
options: Parameters go in, return values come back
Parameters are names, return values are types
They are two words for the same thing
questions.explain: Parameters are the inputs a function receives; the return value is the result it hands back.

questions.ask: The function runs, but coins still prints 25. What is wrong?
options: The returned value is never stored anywhere
The function needs a third argument
questions.explain: awardCoins hands a number back, but nothing catches it. Write coins = awardCoins(coins, 5).

questions.ask: You change a number parameter inside a function. What happens to the caller's variable?
options: Nothing, numbers are values and the parameter is its own name
questions.explain: Parameters are fresh local names for one call. That is exactly why returning the next value works so well.

questions.ask: What do the type annotations actually do?
options: Convert values while the game runs
Tell the type checker your intent so it can warn you
questions.explain: They are a note to your tools and the next reader. They do not convert anything at runtime.

questions.ask: Why prefer returning a new value over changing something distant?
options: The change is visible on the line where it happens, and the function can be tested alone
questions.explain: It makes the state change explicit instead of something you have to go hunting for.

beats.say: A function written inside a scope can see the local variables around it.
More than that, it keeps its connection to them even after the surrounding code has moved on.
A function bundled together with the outer variables it remembers is called a closure.
That sounds abstract until you see what it buys you: a function with a memory. A counter that keeps counting between calls, without you passing the running total in every time.
Here is exactly that.
beats.code:
local score = 0

local function addScore(amount)
    score += amount
    return score
end

print(addScore(10))
print(addScore(5))

beats.say: The name score is declared outside the function. The function reaches out to it, adds to it, and hands the new total back.
Run it and read both numbers. The second call does not start over. It continues from where the first one left off, because both calls share the same score.
Now move that name inside the function and the memory disappears.
beats.code:
local function addScore(amount)
    local score = 0
    score += amount
    return score
end

beats.say: Every call now makes a fresh score, starting at zero. The function still works, but it no longer remembers anything between calls.
So the tool is sharp in both directions.
It is genuinely good for small state that one piece of code clearly owns.
It is a poor choice for anything another part of the game needs to read, check or trust, because that state is now tucked away where nothing else can see it.
Ask who needs to own the truth, and let that answer decide.

questions.ask: What is a closure?
options: A function that closes the program
A function together with the outer variables it remembers
questions.explain: The function holds on to the outer binding, which is what gives it memory between calls.

questions.ask: Every call returns the same small number instead of a growing one. Why?
questions.code:
local function addScore(amount)
    local score = 0
    score += amount
    return score
end
options: score is created fresh inside, so it restarts at zero each call
questions.explain: The variable is born and dies within one call, so there is nothing to remember.

questions.ask: When is a closure the wrong place to keep state?
options: When the value is a number
When another part of the game needs to read or validate it
questions.explain: Closure state is tucked away where nothing else can see it. Ask who needs to own the truth.

questions.ask: A score must be checked by other systems. What is the better shape?
options: Pass the current score in and return the next one
Store it inside the function with local
questions.explain: Explicit state keeps the value visible to whoever needs to trust it.

beats.say: When your code calls a function, the caller pauses and waits.
The called function has to finish and return before the line underneath runs.
Calls stack up and then unwind, like plates stacked and then taken off one at a time.
Recursion is a function that calls itself, each time with a smaller version of the same problem.
It needs a base case: a condition where it stops calling itself and simply returns. Without one, the calls never unwind.
Here is the smallest recursion that still shows the whole shape.
beats.code:
local function countdown(value)
    if value <= 0 then
        print("Go!")
        return
    end

    print(value)
    countdown(value - 1)
end

countdown(3)

beats.say: The first block is the base case. When the value has reached zero there is nothing left to count, so it prints and returns without calling itself again.
Below it, the function prints the current value and calls itself with one less. That is the smaller version of the same problem.
Run it with three and follow the order: three, two, one, then Go. Each call waited for the one it started before it could finish.
Now be honest about when you need this.
For most game scripting, repeating over a known collection, a plain loop is clearer, easier to read and easier to inspect when something goes wrong.
Reach for recursion when the structure itself nests, such as walking a tree of Instances, and when you can state the stopping condition out loud before you write it.

questions.ask: What does a base case do?
options: Stops it, by returning without calling again
questions.explain: The base case returns without another call, which is what lets the whole stack unwind.

questions.ask: This never reaches the end. What is missing?
options: The value passed in never gets smaller
questions.explain: The same value poses the identical problem again, so the base case is never reached.

questions.ask: You need to visit every item in a flat list. What fits best?
questions.explain: For a flat structure a loop is clearer and easier to inspect. Recursion suits structures that nest.

questions.ask: What happens to the caller while a function it called is running?
options: It pauses until the call returns
questions.explain: Calls stack up and then unwind. The caller waits for the return.

beats.say: Section 7 used a list without saying much about what a list actually is. Here is the honest answer.
Luau has one collection type, the table. An array is simply a table used by a shared convention.
The convention is this: values sit at numbered positions, counting up from one, with no gaps.
Two things trip people up early.
The first is that positions start at one, not zero.
The second is subtler and worth taking seriously. The length operator is dependable when the numbered positions are packed together with no holes.
If positions are missing in the middle, the length is not a trustworthy count, and you should not build logic on top of it.
Here is an inventory changed two different ways.
beats.code:
local inventory = {"Sword", "Potion", "Key"}
inventory[2] = "Shield"
table.insert(inventory, "Map")

print(inventory[2])
print(#inventory)

beats.say: The second line replaces what is already at position two. Nothing moves, nothing is added; one slot now holds something else.
The third line adds to the end. The collection grows by one and stays packed.
So the practical takeaway is to keep ordered collections packed. Add with table.insert, remove with table.remove, and do not leave holes behind by assigning nil into the middle.
One more thing to try, because the result surprises people.
beats.code: print(inventory[0])

beats.say: Position zero is not part of the convention. Nothing was ever put there, so nothing comes back.

questions.ask: This returns nil. Why?
options: Array positions start at 1, so there is nothing at 0
The table was never declared local
questions.explain: The convention counts up from 1. The first item is at position 1.

questions.ask: When is the length operator not a trustworthy count?
options: When the table has more than ten items
When the numbered positions have gaps
questions.explain: It is dependable on packed positions. With holes in the middle, do not build logic on it.

questions.ask: What makes a table behave like an array?
options: The keys you choose: consecutive numbers from 1
questions.explain: There is one collection type. The array behaviour comes purely from the keys you use.

questions.ask: How do you keep an ordered collection reliable?
options: Assign nil into the middle to clear slots
Add and remove with the table helpers, leaving no holes
questions.explain: Packed positions keep indexing, insertion and length checks predictable.

beats.say: Position is the right way to organise some things and the wrong way for most others.
Nobody wants to remember that a player's coin count is the second item in a list.
The same table can use meaningful names as keys instead of numbers. Now you ask for coins and get the coin count.
Compare asking for playerState.coins with asking for playerState position one.
The first explains itself. The second forces every future reader, including you, to remember a convention that was never written down.
Here is a small record with two named fields.
Each value is fetched by the name it was stored under. There is no counting and no convention to remember.
Run it and confirm both values arrive. Then add a level field and read it back. Nothing else in the code has to change.
One behaviour to know before you rely on it. Asking for a key that was never set gives you nothing back, rather than an error.
Watch what that costs when you use the missing value straight away.
beats.code: print("Title: " .. playerState.rank)

beats.say: There is no rank in that record. The lookup itself is fine; the failure happens one step later, when the missing value is joined onto text.
That is convenient and it is also a trap, because the problem does not surface where it was caused. Check optional data before treating it as if it is there.

questions.ask: You are storing a player's coins, level and title. Which shape fits?
options: Three separate variables in different files
questions.explain: Names carry the meaning. A position would force readers to remember an unwritten convention.

questions.ask: This fails when joining the text. Why?
options: rank was never set, so it is nil
questions.explain: A key that was never set gives nil, and joining text onto nothing is not meaningful.

questions.ask: What happens when you read a key a table does not have?
options: You get an empty piece of text
questions.explain: It gives nil quietly, which is why optional data should be checked before use.

questions.ask: Which fix is usually better for a missing field?
options: Check for nil at every place it is read
Make whatever creates the record always set the key
questions.explain: Then every record has the same shape and readers can rely on it.

beats.say: Game values usually have edges. Health should not fall below zero. Volume belongs between zero and one. A reward should come from a stated range rather than anywhere at all.
You can enforce edges with a scatter of separate checks, and plenty of code does.
The trouble is that the rule ends up spread across several places, so changing it later means finding all of them and hoping you did.
There is a single call that says the whole rule in one line: here is a value, here is the lowest it may be, here is the highest. It hands back a value inside that range.
Here it is holding health inside its bounds.
beats.code:
local health = -15
local maxHealth = 100
health = math.clamp(health, 0, maxHealth)
print("Health: " .. health)

beats.say: Minus fifteen is below the floor, so what comes back is zero. Anything above maxHealth comes back as maxHealth. Anything already inside passes through untouched.
Try a value above maxHealth and confirm it comes down. Then change maxHealth and predict the result before you run it.
Notice where the rule sits: on the line where the value actually changes. That is exactly where a reader will look for it.
The argument order carries the meaning, so getting it wrong does not fail loudly.
beats.code: math.clamp(0, maxHealth, health)

beats.say: That reads as: take zero, keep it between maxHealth and health. It is a valid call and a wrong question.

questions.ask: This does not produce the number expected. What is wrong?
options: The arguments are in the wrong order
questions.explain: The value comes first, then the minimum, then the maximum. State first, rule second.

questions.ask: health is -15 and maxHealth is 100. What does math.clamp(health, 0, maxHealth) give?
questions.explain: The value is below the minimum, so it comes back as the minimum. The range includes both ends.

questions.ask: Why is clamp better than several separate checks?
options: The rule lives in one place, where the value actually changes
questions.explain: Scattered checks mean changing the rule later requires finding all of them.

questions.ask: Where should randomness be kept away from?
questions.explain: That is a design and trust question long before it is a coding one.

beats.say: The table library gives you operations that name what you are doing: insert, remove, clear, clone.
Using the one that matches your intent beats rebuilding a collection by hand and hoping the side effects work out.
When a collection holds game state, get into the habit of looking at it before and after a change.
A removal that silently does nothing, or removes the wrong thing, is much easier to catch when you can see both sides of it.
Here is an item being used, with the used item kept.
beats.code:
local inventory = {"Potion", "Key", "Map"}
local usedItem = table.remove(inventory, 1)

print("Used: " .. usedItem)
print("Remaining: " .. #inventory)

beats.say: Removing hands back what it removed. That is why the item can be reported rather than lost.
Now the behaviour that matters more than the rest here. Removing from the middle of a packed array does not leave a hole.
Everything after the removed position shifts down to close the gap. That is usually what you want, and it is also the source of a classic bug.
Here is that bug.
beats.code:
table.remove(inventory, 1)
print(inventory[2])

beats.say: Position two no longer holds what it held a moment ago. Everything moved down by one when the first item left.
Nothing is broken. The collection did exactly what it promised. The mistake is reading a position that was captured before the shift.

questions.ask: What does table.remove hand back?
questions.explain: Catching it turns a deletion into a transaction: the item is in your hand, not just gone.

questions.ask: After removing the first item, position 2 holds something unexpected. Why?
options: A packed array closes gaps, so later items shifted down
questions.explain: Everything after the removed item moves down one, so remembered positions no longer match.

questions.ask: A thing's identity matters more than where it sits. What should you do?
options: Give it a name and use a keyed table
questions.explain: Positions shift. Names do not.

questions.ask: Why check a collection before and after changing it?
options: A removal that does nothing, or the wrong thing, is much easier to catch
questions.explain: Seeing both sides makes the change observable instead of assumed.

beats.say: To understand how Luau handles text, imagine a library where every book is carved into a permanent stone tablet.
Once a string is written, it can never be altered.
If you want to change the word Cat to Cats, you cannot carve an s onto the end of the existing tablet.
You must carve an entirely new tablet containing the word Cats. The old Cat tablet stays as it was, until nobody needs it any more.
That is what immutability means here, and it is not a restriction for its own sake.
The library has a second rule: only one copy of any unique word is allowed to exist.
Ask the librarian for Apple, and they check a master index. If Apple has already been carved, they hand you a slip of paper pointing at that existing tablet.
Which makes comparing two words for sameness extremely fast. The librarian does not read both tablets letter by letter. They check whether both slips point at the same shelf.
The practical consequence is the one to carry with you. Building a long piece of text by adding to it repeatedly does not extend anything.
Each addition carves a fresh tablet and discards the last one. Do that inside a loop and you have made a pile of tablets nobody asked for.

questions.ask: You change the word Cat to Cats. What actually happens?
options: The letter s is appended to the existing string
A brand new string is created
The string is edited in place to save memory
Nothing, strings cannot change at all
questions.explain: Strings are immutable. Changing one always means building a new one.

questions.ask: Why is comparing two identical strings so fast in Luau?
options: It compares letter by letter very quickly
Only one copy of a unique string exists, so it compares which tablet they point at
It compares only the first letter
questions.explain: Interning means identical text is stored once, so comparison checks identity rather than contents.

questions.ask: You build a sentence by joining onto the same variable inside a loop that runs a thousand times. What is the cost?
options: Nothing, it is the normal way
Around a thousand intermediate strings are created and thrown away
The loop runs a thousand times faster
questions.explain: Each join copies everything so far into a new string and discards the old one.

questions.ask: What is the fix for building a long string piece by piece?
options: Collect the pieces in a table and join them once at the end
questions.explain: One join at the end means one new string instead of hundreds.

questions.ask: What do backticks let you do that double quotes do not?
options: Write variables directly inside the text in curly braces
questions.explain: That is string interpolation, a shorter alternative to string.format.

beats.say: Imagine you are a customs inspector in a busy shipping port. Thousands of cargo crates pass your station every day, and each crate is a piece of text.
Your job is to check whether a crate contains something specific: a passport with exactly five digits, or a word that starts with a capital letter.
You could hire a team to open and catalogue every single item. That is what heavy regular expression engines do, and it slows the port down.
Instead you use a short checklist with shorthand codes.
Rather than writing check for a, b, c and so on to z, you write one code that means a lowercase letter. Another means a digit.
Capitalising a code inverts it. Where one code means find a digit, its capital means find anything that is not a digit.
Then there is the question of how much an inspector grabs.

A greedy inspector wants the largest match possible. Tell them to find everything between angle brackets, hand them a line with several pairs, and they will take from the first opening bracket all the way to the last closing one.
That is usually not what you meant. The polite variant stops at the first closing bracket instead, which is almost always the intent.
This is worth learning properly because parsing text badly is a quiet kind of bug. It does not crash. It just returns the wrong slice, and everything downstream believes it.

questions.ask: What does the shorthand code for a digit become when you capitalise it?
options: It matches anything that is not a digit
questions.explain: Capitalising a class inverts it. That is the inversion key.

questions.ask: Your pattern swallowed far more text than expected. What is the likely cause?
options: A greedy quantifier took the largest possible match
questions.explain: Greedy quantifiers reach for the largest match. The polite form stops at the minimum.

questions.ask: You want a match to stop at the first closing bracket, not the last. What do you need?
questions.explain: The polite form satisfies the minimum and stops.

questions.ask: How does Luau's pattern matching differ from a heavy regular expression engine?
options: It is more powerful in every way
It is deliberately lightweight and fast rather than exhaustive
It is slower but more accurate
questions.explain: It is designed as a small, fast inspector rather than a large general engine.

beats.say: We treat data as flexible, but underneath, computer memory has strict rules. Two ways of writing information down make the difference clear.
A string is a printing press. You want the word CAT, so the press stamps CAT onto a strip of paper.
Now change it to CAR. You cannot erase the T. The press runs again, stamps a brand new strip reading CAR, and the old strip goes in the bin.
Do that hundreds of times a second and you have made a mountain of paper that the computer must keep clearing away.
A buffer is the other thing entirely: a pre-built grid of dry-erase slots, each exactly large enough to hold one number.
To change the number in slot three, you wipe that slot and write a new one. The grid never changes size, no paper is produced, and no cleanup crew is ever called.
So the two are not competitors. They are for different jobs.
Text that a person reads belongs in a string. Numbers that change constantly, especially many of them, belong in a buffer.
The reason this sits in the course at all is the cleanup crew. Work that generates constant rubbish costs you frames, and frames are what a player actually feels.

questions.ask: What is the key difference between a string and a buffer?
options: Buffers hold text, strings hold numbers
A buffer's slots can be overwritten in place; a string must be recreated
questions.explain: A buffer is a fixed workspace you rewrite. A string is stamped once and replaced when changed.

questions.ask: When is a buffer the right tool?
options: When rewriting the same slots repeatedly without generating waste
questions.explain: Allocate once, overwrite many times, without leaving discarded copies behind.

questions.ask: What does allocating a buffer give you?
questions.explain: The size is fixed up front, which is exactly what avoids repeated allocation.

beats.say: Imagine a control board with exactly thirty two light switches in a row, numbered from left to right.
Each switch has two positions, on or off, and nothing in between.
Numbers are normally ordinary decimal values. When you use the bitwise library, the computer temporarily reads your number as that row of switches.
Now suppose you have two boards and want to combine them into a third.
The and operation turns a switch on only when that exact switch is on for both boards. If either is off, the result is off.
The or operation turns a switch on when at least one of the boards has it on.
The exclusive or asks whether the two boards disagree. One on and one off gives on. Both the same gives off.
And the not operation takes a single board and flips every switch to its opposite.
What is this for? Storing many yes-or-no facts in one number, and comparing them all in a single operation instead of one at a time.
Which is exactly the shape of things like permissions and collision rules, where a long list of small truths has to travel together.

questions.ask: A switch is on in one board and off in the other. What does AND produce for it?
questions.explain: AND turns a switch on only when both inputs have it on.

questions.ask: What does exclusive OR actually test?
options: Whether the boards are the same length
questions.explain: It turns the result on when the two inputs differ, and off when they match.

questions.ask: What is the difference between a shift and a rotate?
options: A shift loses the switches that fall off; a rotate wraps them round
A shift only works on positive numbers
questions.explain: Rotation preserves every switch by wrapping it to the other end.

questions.ask: How does arithmetic shift right differ from an ordinary shift right?
options: It clones the leftmost state instead of always filling with off
questions.explain: That is what preserves the sign of a negative number.

beats.say: Imagine you are a single chef cooking a complex dinner, with three things to prepare: bread to bake, soup to simmer, and vegetables to chop.
You have one set of hands, which is one processor. You cannot physically do all three in the same millisecond.
So you work cooperatively rather than trying to do everything at once.
You mix the dough, put it in the oven, and pause your work on the bread while it bakes.
While the bread bakes you switch to the soup, turn on the heat, and pause again to let it simmer.
While the soup simmers you chop the vegetables. When the oven timer goes, you resume the bread exactly where you left it.
That is what a coroutine is. Not a second chef, which would be true parallelism, but one worker who can put a task down and pick it up again without losing their place.
The word to hold on to is cooperative. A coroutine is never interrupted; it hands control back when it chooses to.
That is a real advantage: nothing can be halfway through changing something when another task starts. It also means one task that never yields blocks everything behind it.

questions.ask: How does a coroutine differ from true parallel execution?
options: One thread pauses and resumes tasks rather than several running at once
questions.explain: One chef, switching between recipes, not three chefs cooking simultaneously.

questions.ask: What does yielding do?
options: Pauses it so it can be resumed later from the same place
questions.explain: The pause keeps its place, which is what lets you pick it back up.

questions.ask: A coroutine has finished, or errored. What state is it in?
questions.explain: Dead means it cannot be worked on any more, whether it completed or failed.

questions.ask: What does the Normal state mean?
options: It is waiting on a sub task it requested
questions.explain: Normal is the state of a coroutine that is currently waiting on another one it called.

beats.say: Imagine ordinary English text as a train where every cargo car is exactly one metre long.
To find the fifth car you measure five metres down the track, and you are exactly at its start. That is how plain ASCII text works: one character is one byte.
Now picture international text, with emoji, Kanji or Arabic script, as a train whose cars have different lengths.
A plain letter is still one metre. A complex Chinese character might be three. A smiley face might be four.
Try to find the fifth character by measuring five metres and you may cut straight through the middle of a four-metre car.
What you get back is not a shorter piece of text. It is a broken one: a byte sequence that is not a character at all.
The UTF-8 library is the inspector who walks the train instead of measuring it. It identifies where each car actually starts and ends.
So the rule is short. The moment text can contain anything a player typed, counting by bytes is guessing, and this library is how you stop guessing.

questions.ask: Why can counting bytes go wrong with international text?
options: Characters can take different numbers of bytes, so a byte offset may land mid-character
questions.explain: Cars have different lengths, so measuring distance can cut one in half.

questions.ask: What does the utf8 library actually do for you?
options: Finds where each character truly starts and ends
questions.explain: It walks the train rather than blindly measuring, so characters stay intact.

questions.ask: When should you stop reasoning about text in bytes?
options: As soon as the text can contain anything beyond plain English
Only when saving to a file
questions.explain: Player-entered text in a real game routinely contains exactly that.

beats.say: Picture your running code as a busy office building.
Each time a function is called, a new floor is built on top. Inside that floor the local variables live and the work happens.
If that function calls another one, another floor goes up on top of it. That stack of floors is the call stack.
The debug library is a detective who can inspect the building while it is still running, with two tools.
The first is a clipboard. It lets you ask a worker on the third floor: what is your name, which file did you come from, how many parameters did you arrive with.
The same clipboard can take the lift from the top floor down to the lobby, writing down every floor it passes. That is a traceback: exactly how the code got to where it is.
The second tool is a stopwatch. You put a start sticker at the beginning of an expensive task and a stop sticker at the end, and the engine reports how long the work between them took.
That is the honest way to find slow code. Reading a function and deciding it looks expensive is a guess; timing it is a measurement.
And measurement is the whole point of this section. Everything here answers a question about a program that is already running, rather than one you are imagining.

questions.ask: What does a traceback give you?
options: The list of calls that led to the current point
questions.explain: It is the ride from the top floor to the lobby, recording every floor passed.

questions.ask: What do profilebegin and profileend let you do?
options: Measure how long the work between them takes
questions.explain: Start and stop stickers around an expensive task, with the engine reporting the time.

questions.ask: You think a part of your game is slow. What should you do first?
options: Measure it, because guessing is unreliable
Remove features until it is fast
questions.explain: Measuring turns a hunch into a fact before you spend effort on it.

questions.ask: In the office building picture, what is a new floor?
options: A function call, with its own local variables
questions.explain: Each call stacks a floor holding that call's own locals.

beats.say: Imagine a factory that packs toy boxes. Before anything ships, you want every box to contain exactly what the label says.
The type checker is your quality control inspector, and you choose how strict they are with one line at the top of a script.
On the loosest setting the inspector is blindfolded. They check only that boxes are sealed and not broken, which is the grammar of your code.
They never look inside. A box labelled Action Figure containing a banana goes out of the door.
The middle setting is the default, and the inspector is casual. They look inside, but they are relaxed about it.
They will stop you doing something obviously dangerous, but they let a lot of quieter mismatches through.
The strictest setting is the inspector who checks every label against every content, and says so when a box arrives unlabelled.
Here is the part worth understanding before you pick one. Stricter is not automatically better on day one.
On a codebase written without types, the strict inspector reports a great many things at once, and a wall of complaints is easy to ignore.
The setting is per file, which is the point. You can tighten one script that matters without stopping the rest of the game from running.

questions.ask: Which mode is the default?
questions.explain: Non strict is the casual inspector: it looks inside but is relaxed about unlabelled things.

questions.ask: What does no check mode actually verify?
options: Only that the code is grammatically valid
questions.explain: The blindfolded inspector confirms the box is sealed, which is the syntax check, not the contents.

questions.ask: You want the most mistakes caught before shipping. Which mode?
questions.explain: The perfectionist holds exact blueprints, so everything must match its label.

beats.say: Picture solving a logic puzzle. Rather than guessing an answer for each space, you first write down the clues.
The red house belongs to the painter. The painter owns a dog. The person in the blue house owns a cat.
At first you know nothing about who lives where. But once the clues are collected, you look at how they connect.
Combine the first two and a new fact appears that nobody stated: the red house has a dog.
That is exactly how the type checker works, and it is worth knowing because it explains the error messages.
Reading your code, it does not immediately decide whether things are correct. It collects clues.
Seeing a value set to five, it writes down a clue: this name holds a number. It does not stop to check anything yet.
Only afterwards does it sit down with the whole collection and work out what follows.
Which is why a complaint sometimes points at a line that looks innocent. That line is where two clues finally contradicted each other, not necessarily where the mistake was made.

questions.ask: How does the type checker work through your code?
options: It checks each line as it reads it
It collects constraints first, then solves them together
questions.explain: Clues are gathered first; the deduction happens once they can be combined.

questions.ask: Why can an error point at a line that looks fine alone?
options: The contradiction only appears once several constraints are combined
questions.explain: A single clue is consistent; the conflict emerges from the combination.

questions.ask: You never wrote a type, yet the checker knows one. Why?
options: It deduced it from the constraints around it
questions.explain: Same as deducing who owns the cat: the answer follows from the clues.

beats.say: Have you ever tried to put a square peg in a round hole, or poured salt into a cake instead of sugar?
Types exist to prevent that kind of mix-up, by labelling what each piece of information actually is.
Think of every value in your program as a toy, and a type as the label on it.
Some toys are basic. A true-or-false value is a light switch: on or off, nothing else.
A number is a counting block. It is always a quantity.
A piece of text is a name tag. It is always writing.
Sometimes you need several toys grouped together, and that is a table.
You can describe the shape of that group in advance: this box contains a name, which is text, and a score, which is a number.
Now anything claiming to be that kind of box has to have those things, in those shapes.
That is the whole idea. A type is a promise about shape, written down where a reader and the checker can both see it.

questions.ask: What is a type, in this picture?
options: A label saying what kind of thing it is
questions.explain: The label on the toy, so mismatches are caught before they cause trouble.

questions.ask: Which describes a boolean?
options: A light switch with two positions
questions.explain: True or false, on or off, nothing in between.

questions.ask: What does the type of a table describe?
options: Its shape: which named parts it has and what each holds
questions.explain: Grouping toys together means describing the group's shape.

beats.say: Sometimes you need precise rules about what is allowed where. There are two shapes of rule, and confusing them is the usual mistake.
The first is a union: this or that.
Picture a container that may hold either a piece of fruit or a number. An apple is fine. The number five is fine. A shoe is not.
Something optional is the same idea. A phone number you might provide means: a number, or nothing at all.
The second is an intersection: this and that, at the same time.
Imagine needing a toy that is both red and round. A red square will not do. A blue circle will not do.
It must have every characteristic you asked for simultaneously.
So the two read almost identically in English and mean opposite things about how much is allowed.
A union widens what may arrive and narrows what you may assume. An intersection narrows what may arrive and widens what you may assume.

questions.ask: A union of fruit or number: what can go in?
options: Either a fruit or a number, but not a shoe
questions.explain: This or that, and nothing outside the listed options.

questions.ask: How is an optional value described?
options: As a union of the value and nothing
questions.explain: A phone number you might provide is the number, or nothing at all.

questions.ask: What does an intersection require?
options: At least one part to hold
Every part to hold at once
questions.explain: This and that, satisfied together.

questions.ask: What is a singleton type for?
options: One exact value, such as a named state
questions.explain: Exactly this, which is how a small set of named states is described.

beats.say: Imagine building a box specifically for apples, and then a completely separate box for oranges, and another for anything else you might store.
A generic is one smart box instead.
Put an apple in it and it becomes an apple box: from then on it accepts apples and hands back apples.
Put a toy car in and it becomes a toy car box.
The type it holds is decided the first time you use it, and it sticks to that decision afterwards, which is what stops apples and toy cars getting mixed.
A type pack is the same instinct applied to sequences rather than single values.
Picture a conveyor belt that takes items in and sends items out. Sometimes one item, sometimes three, sometimes five.
A type pack lets you describe whatever sequence arrives, rather than writing a separate rule for every possible length.
Both exist for the same reason: to write a rule once and have it hold for many shapes, instead of copying the rule and hoping the copies stay in step.

questions.ask: What does a generic container give you?
options: One container that adapts, remembering what went in
A container that holds anything with no type
questions.explain: One smart box rather than one per kind, and it keeps track of the kind.

questions.ask: Why is remembering the type important?
options: What comes out is known, rather than becoming a vague anything
questions.explain: Losing the type is exactly what a generic prevents.

questions.ask: What is a type pack for?
options: A whole group of values at once
questions.explain: That is what makes it work for functions taking or returning several things.

beats.say: Imagine a container that might hold a fruit, or a vegetable, or nothing at all. You cannot tell by looking at the outside.
That uncertainty is the broad type. It covers every possibility, honestly, which is exactly why you cannot do much with it.
To use what is inside you need to know which it is. You cannot peel a carrot or chop a banana and expect a good result.
Narrowing is the act of finding out and having the checker remember.
You do it with a check. Ask whether the thing is a banana, and inside the branch where the answer was yes, it is a banana.
Not might be. Is. The checker follows the same reasoning you just did, and stops complaining about the possibilities you ruled out.
The commonest version of this is checking whether something exists at all before using it.
Which is why this pairs so directly with the earlier warning about asking for a key that was never set. Narrowing is how that warning stops being a trap.

questions.ask: What is narrowing?
options: Establishing which case of a union you actually have
questions.explain: From mystery item to known item, so specific actions become safe.

questions.ask: What is a type guard?
options: A check that tells you which case you have
questions.explain: The scanner that confirms it is a banana, which the checker then trusts inside that branch.

questions.ask: The checker rejects code you are sure is correct. What is it saying?
options: Nothing in the code has established which case you are in
questions.explain: Your certainty is not visible to it. A guard makes it visible.

beats.say: Your program likes to categorise everything: numbers, text, true or false, and objects of various kinds. Those categories are the types.
Sometimes it works the category out on its own. Sometimes it needs telling.
Telling it is like relabelling a box. You have one marked Stuff from the garage, and you happen to know it contains car parts.
So you say so, with a double colon, and from then on the program treats it as car parts.
Now the part that matters more than the syntax. You have not changed what is in the box.
An assertion changes what the checker believes, not what is true. If the box really held garden tools, nothing complains at that moment, and something goes wrong later.
So the honest use is narrow: you genuinely know something the checker cannot, and you are willing to own it.
Reaching for it because the checker is being inconvenient is how a type system quietly stops protecting you.

questions.ask: What does a type assertion actually do?
options: States a promise you are making to the checker
questions.explain: It is a label you apply, not a verification. A wrong promise is not caught.

questions.ask: You join text with a number and it works. What happened?
options: The number was silently converted to text
questions.explain: That silent adjustment is coercion.

questions.ask: Why are assertions risky?
options: If the promise is wrong, nothing catches it
questions.explain: You have overridden the checker, so the responsibility is yours.

beats.say: Imagine a complex recipe written in plain English, full of description and natural phrasing.
You would not hand that to a fast robot chef. You would first have it translated into something the robot follows exactly.
That is what happens to your Luau. What you write is the English recipe: readable, with words and loops and function calls.
The compiler is the translator, and it works in steps.
First it reads the recipe word by word, deciding what each piece is: a name, a number, a piece of punctuation doing a job.
Then it works out the structure those pieces form, which turns a flat line of words into something with shape.
Then it writes the robot's version: a long list of tiny, exact instructions.
That list is the bytecode, and it is what actually runs. Your source file is not executed; its translation is.
Worth knowing for one practical reason. It explains why some mistakes are caught before anything runs at all, and others only when the robot reaches that instruction.

questions.ask: What does the lexer do?
options: Identifies the individual words and symbols
questions.explain: Word by word, without understanding the structure yet.

questions.ask: And the parser?
options: Works out the grammar and structure
questions.explain: It turns a list of words into an understood instruction.

questions.ask: You wrote one plus one as a constant. What does the optimiser do?
options: Computes it ahead of time and stores two
questions.explain: Work that can be settled before running does not need doing every time.

questions.ask: What does the virtual machine actually receive?
options: Bytecode, a compact list of exact instructions
questions.explain: The human phrasing has already been resolved away by then.

beats.say: Picture your computer as a busy office. Every time a function runs, a worker takes on a new task.
To work, they need a workspace. A desk. In these terms that desk is the stack, and it holds everything belonging to that one task while it happens.
Luau is a tidy worker. Rather than piling everything onto the desk, it uses labelled bins arranged on it.
Those bins are registers, and one is always reserved to remind the worker which task they are currently on.
The rest hold the materials: the values that came in, and the intermediate results produced along the way.
The reason this design is worth a section is speed. Reaching into a labelled bin is faster than searching a pile.
And it is why the number of local values a function juggles is not a free choice, though you will rarely meet the limit while writing ordinary game code.
The practical takeaway is simply this: locals are cheap because they live in bins on the desk, and that is why the course keeps recommending them.

questions.ask: What is the stack, in this picture?
questions.explain: The desk belonging to the task currently being worked on.

questions.ask: What are registers?
options: Labelled bins holding the values a function is working with
questions.explain: Directly in front of the worker, rather than piled on the desk.

questions.ask: Why does this arrangement matter?
options: Reaching a labelled bin is far faster than searching
questions.explain: Speed is the whole reason for the arrangement.

beats.say: The robot chef from earlier does not understand human recipes. It needs tiny, exact instructions in a simplified language.
Those instructions are the opcodes, and the machine reading them is the virtual machine.
It works with three things.
A recipe book: the long list of instructions that make up your program.
Small labelled containers on the counter, for holding ingredients while it works. Those are the registers from the previous section.
And a pantry of things that never change, such as fixed numbers and pieces of text that appear in your code.
Every line you write becomes some sequence of these instructions: move this into that container, add these two, call the thing in that container.
You will not write opcodes. The value of seeing them is realising there is no magic left at the bottom, only a short list of very small operations done very quickly.

questions.ask: What is an opcode?
options: One tiny instruction for the virtual machine
questions.explain: The chef reads one, acts, moves on.

questions.ask: What lives in the constant table?
options: Values that never change, so they are not rebuilt each time
questions.explain: The pantry of pre made ingredients.

questions.ask: What is the auxiliary word for?
options: Carrying extra detail when an instruction will not fit on one line
questions.explain: A note attached to an instruction that needs more room.

beats.say: Picture Luau as a chef, and every piece of data as an ingredient: a number, a piece of text, a true or false answer.
To keep the kitchen efficient the chef puts every single ingredient into the same standardised container.
Every box is exactly the same size, whatever is inside. That is the point of it.
Same size means the chef can grab, move and store any ingredient without measuring anything first.
Each box has two parts.
The main space holds the ingredient itself, big enough for the small kinds of value.
And a label says which kind of ingredient this is, so the box can be read correctly.
Which is the answer to a question you may not have known you had: how can one name hold a number now and a piece of text later?
Because the container never changed. Only the label and the contents did.

questions.ask: What are the two parts of every value box?
options: A tag saying what kind, and the value or a pointer to it
questions.explain: Type and value, which is what TValue stands for.

questions.ask: Where does a table live?
options: Elsewhere, with the box holding a pointer to it
questions.explain: Complex ingredients are too big for the box, so the box points at them.

questions.ask: Why is every box the same size?
options: Moving a value never requires asking how big it is
questions.explain: Uniformity is what makes the machine fast.

beats.say: Imagine memory as a giant library, and every piece of data your program uses as a book.
As the program runs it keeps creating books, and stops using others. Without tidying, the library fills with books nobody will open again.
The garbage collector is the librarian who keeps it usable.
The first thing worth knowing is how they work: in shifts.
Rather than closing the library for a day, which would freeze your game, they tidy a small section at a time while people are still reading.
The second is how they decide what to keep, and it is a three-colour system.
Everything starts as not yet looked at. Anything reachable from the program gets marked as to be examined, and then as examined and kept.
When the pass finishes, whatever is still in the first group was reachable from nothing at all, and its space can be reused.
Which is exactly why a forgotten connection is such a problem. It is a reference, so the librarian keeps the book, and no amount of tidying will reclaim it.

questions.ask: Why does the collector work in shifts?
options: Doing it all at once would freeze the game
questions.explain: Closing the whole library at once is exactly the stall it avoids.

questions.ask: What does a grey book mean?
options: It is in use, but what it refers to has not been checked yet
questions.explain: Noticed as reachable, but its own references are still unexamined.

questions.ask: What happens to something still white at the end of a sweep?
options: It was unreachable, so it is cleared away
questions.explain: Nothing reachable was left white by the time the sweep finished.

questions.ask: How does the collector decide something is still needed?
options: By how recently it was made
By whether it can still be reached from what definitely matters
questions.explain: The sweep starts from the roots and works outward.

beats.say: This is the library from the string section, seen from the inside.
When your code uses the same word repeatedly, making a fresh copy each time would be waste.
So there is a rule: for every unique word or phrase, exactly one master copy exists.
Ask for a word and the librarian checks a special shelf first.
If it is already there, you are pointed at the existing copy rather than given a new one.
If it is not, it gets carved once and added to the shelf, and every later request is pointed at that.
Two consequences follow, and both are useful.
Comparing two pieces of text for sameness is fast, because it is a comparison of shelf locations rather than of letters.
And building many one-off pieces of text is more expensive than it looks, because each new unique one has to be added to the shelf.

questions.ask: How many copies of a unique piece of text exist?
questions.explain: That single rule is what interning means.

questions.ask: Why does interning make comparison fast?
options: It compares which master copy each points at, not the characters
It compares only the first letter
questions.explain: One comparison, regardless of how long the text is.

questions.ask: What is the other benefit?
questions.explain: One physical copy rather than one per use.

beats.say: Think of your script as a recipe and the machine as a kitchen.
Normally an assistant reads your recipe one step at a time and tells the kitchen what to do. Careful, correct, and always going through the reading step.
Native execution is a different mode. The recipe goes to a master chef who already knows the techniques.
Rather than reading each step and then performing it, they translate the whole thing into direct actions and carry them out.
The gain is real, and it is not free of conditions.
It helps most where the same arithmetic runs enormously often, which is the shape of physics and heavy numeric work.
It helps least where the work is mostly calls out to the engine, because the time is being spent on the other side of that boundary anyway.
So it is a tool to reach for after measuring, not before. Which is exactly what the debug library's stopwatch was for.

questions.ask: What does ahead of time compilation mean here?
options: Learning the recipe as orders arrive
Understanding the whole recipe before any cooking begins
questions.explain: Just in time is the other one, and it is not permitted on some platforms.

questions.ask: Where should native execution be used?
options: On measured hot paths where the work justifies it
questions.explain: The preparation has a cost, so it pays off only where the work is heavy.

questions.ask: What is the actual gain?
options: The machine acts directly rather than consulting instructions each step
questions.explain: That is the difference between the assistant and the master chef.

beats.say: Two friends need to build something together. One speaks C plus plus, the other speaks Luau.
They cannot simply shout instructions at each other, because neither understands the other's language.
So they use a shared workspace: a message board made of a stack of sticky notes.
When the C plus plus side wants to pass something over, a number or a piece of text, it writes a note and puts it on the board. That is pushing.
When the Luau side needs it, it reads the notes and takes them off. That is popping.
Everything crossing the boundary goes through that board, in a known order. There is no second channel and no shortcut.
That constraint is the reason the rest of this unit looks the way it does.
Every property you read and every method you call on a Roblox object is, underneath, notes going onto that board and coming back off it.

questions.ask: How do the two sides exchange values?
options: Through a shared stack, pushing and popping notes
questions.explain: The message board is the only channel across the boundary.

questions.ask: What does pushing mean?
options: Placing a value onto the shared stack
questions.explain: Writing a note and putting it on the board.

beats.say: Luau is a chef. C plus plus is a factory producing special ingredients: game objects, tools, complex data.
The chef needs to use those ingredients without knowing how the factory made them.
Userdata is how the factory hands them over. It is a package the Luau side can hold and use like any other value.
With a full userdata the factory sends a complete, brand new item. Luau owns it from then on.
Owning it means Luau also knows when nobody needs it any more, and can clean it up.
Each package can arrive with its own instruction manual attached.
Which is why two engine objects can respond differently to the same request: they are not the same kind of thing, and their manuals say so.
The result is that a Roblox object feels like an ordinary Luau value while actually living on the engine side of the board.

questions.ask: What is userdata?
options: The way engine-side objects are handed to Luau
questions.explain: The package the factory sends to the chef.

questions.ask: Who cleans up a full userdata?
options: Luau, once nothing needs it any more
questions.explain: Luau owns it, so its collector handles it.

questions.ask: Why can two engine objects behave differently to the same request?
options: Each can carry its own instruction manual
questions.explain: That per-object manual is what makes them feel like distinct kinds.

beats.say: You speak Luau. The Roblox engine speaks C plus plus. Something has to translate between you.
That translator is the reflection engine, sitting between your script and the engine's inner workings.
It carries a large dictionary, holding every detail about every property and method the engine exposes.
Ask a part for its position and you are really asking the translator a question.
It looks up Position for a Part, works out where the real value lives, fetches it, and hands it back.
Every property access crosses that boundary. It is fast, but it is not free.
Which is exactly why reading the same property repeatedly inside a hot loop can cost more than the work the loop is doing.
Read it once, keep it in a local, and the crossing happens once instead of a thousand times.

questions.ask: What does the reflection engine do?
options: Translates between Luau and the engine's internals
questions.explain: It is the translator, with a dictionary of everything the engine exposes.

questions.ask: Why can repeated property access in a tight loop be costly?
